get.summary: `{ id, substrate, health, limitations }` where `health` is `up`, `starting`, `unresponsive` or `down`, read from the substrate itself (`sbx ls` for a microVM). `limitations` repeats what the workshop lacks, such as a bare host running commands unconfined.

502.description: The substrate's own command failed; `error` carries what it said.

503.description: This host serves no workshops, or the workshop's substrate is not available here.

post.summary: A typed terminal into one workshop: run `command` with the workshop's own shell from its workdir (or `cwd` inside it), through the same substrate exec the creature's `bash` tool uses, so it carries the same jail, the same broker sentinels and never a real credential, and answer `{ workshop, code, stdout, stderr, timedOut }`. A microVM workshop takes typed commands unless a keeper rule says otherwise; a bare host workshop runs them on this node itself, so it refuses with 403 until the keeper grants the rule `{ action: "workshop.exec", resource: "<workshop id>" | "<creature>" | "*", effect: "allow" }` in the workspace or user permissions; the last matching rule decides and an `ask` refuses, since a typed terminal cannot ask. Every command, run or refused, is logged as a keeper tool call in the workshop's terminal log; refusals also land in its refusal log. Output is answered, never stored.

200.description: `{ workshop, code, stdout, stderr, timedOut }`; a non-zero `code` is the command's own.

400.description: The body is not `{ command, cwd?, timeoutMs? }`.

403.description: The keeper has not granted typed commands into this workshop; `error` says which rule would.

409.description: The workshop is not running.

502.description: The substrate's own command failed; `error` carries what it said.

503.description: This host serves no workshops, or the workshop's substrate is not available here.

get.summary: The workshop's virtual display as a snapshot stream: server-sent `event: frame` with `data: { png, at }` once a second, `png` being a base64 PNG scaled to at most 1024x768. The stream ends with `event: ended` when the display goes away (no Xvfb in the workshop) and closes when the client leaves. View only; nothing here can type or click.

503.description: The workshop has no display (a bare host workshop never does), or no workshops are served.

get.summary: This node's pairing state: `{ claim, owner, pairs, pending }`. `claim` is `unclaimed` until the first console pairs; `owner` is the `(tailnetId, userId)` of the human who claimed it; `pairs` are the peers this node trusts, each `{ id, peerStableId, peerUserId, peerTags, role, caps, endpoint, createdAt, confirmedBy }` where `role` is `console` (may issue grants here), `node` (may call with grants) or `target` (this node is its console); `pending` lists inbound attempts with the six-digit `sas` to compare.

post.summary: Start pairing this console with a node found by discovery: sends the hello and the nonce reveal, then answers `{ attemptId, sas, confirmation, expiresAt }`. Show `sas` to the keeper; `confirmation` says what the target needs (`on-device`, a `claim-code`, or an `endorsement` from a console already paired there).

endpoint.description: The node's mesh base URL, e.g. http://100.88.77.66:47800.

stableId.description: The node's StableID as WhoIs reports it.

400.description: The body is not a pairing request.

502.description: The node refused or answered badly; `failed` says why.

post.summary: Finish an attempt this console began. `matches: false` cancels it on both sides; `matches: true` sends the confirmation (with `claimCode` for a headless host) and waits for the target's own confirmation, then stores the pair key and answers `{ paired }`.

409.description: The attempt ended without a pair; `failed` says why.

post.summary: The keeper at this machine confirms an inbound attempt after comparing the SAS on both screens; `sas` is the code this node showed.

200.description: `{ state }`: `confirming` until the console confirms, then `paired`.

409.description: The attempt aborted; `reason` says why.

delete.summary: Forget a pair here at once. When this node is the peer's console, a signed revocation is pushed to the peer and retried until it lands.

get.summary: Live grants: `{ issued, installed }`. `issued` are grants this console signed for creatures to act on other nodes; `installed` are grants other consoles signed that let creatures act here. Each is `{ id, issuer, subject: { creature, node }, target, caps, issuedAt, expiresAt, nonce, signature }`.

post.summary: Sign a grant with this console's device key and push it to the target node, which verifies the chain to a paired owner console and renders `files:*` and `exec` caps into rules scoped to the creature. Caps: `{ kind: files:read | files:write, paths }`, `{ kind: exec, commands }` (literal command heads), `{ kind: screen:view | screen:control | clipboard }`.

target.description: The StableID of the node the creature may act on.

400.description: The draft is not a grant.

403.description: The target refused it.

404.description: This console is not paired with the target.

delete.summary: Revoke a grant here at once and push a signed revocation to the target, retried until it lands.

404.description: No live grant has that id.

get.summary: This node's hash-chained audit rows: `{ rows, chain }`, each row `{ ts, actorStableID, actorUserID, actorTags, targetStableID, capability, requestDigest, decision, reason, prevHash, hash }`. Rows come oldest first; `?order=newest` turns the page newest first, so its first page holds the latest rows. `?after=<hash>` continues from a known row in the page's order (older rows when newest first) and `?limit=` caps the page; `chain` reports whether the whole log still verifies.

400.description: `order` is neither `oldest` nor `newest`.

post.summary: Chain one screen row into this node's audit log, posted by the console that shared the screen. `kind: control` records a control grant decided over a live view (`decision`, `reason` in words, `expiresAt`); `kind: session` records a finished session with its grant, `scopes` (`view`, or `view` and `control`), `displays`, `path`, `startedAt`, `endedAt`, the end `reason` and the injected input counts. The row's capability is `screen:control` when control was held or asked, `screen:view` otherwise; its reason says every field in words and its `requestDigest` binds the record. A creature may control only its own workshop's display, so the console records an agent's request to control a keeper's desktop as a `deny` row.

400.description: The body is not a screen audit record.

post.summary: One creature messages another, here or on a paired machine: plain text, delivered into the conversation of the receiving creature as one creature-origin line (`Message from <sender> on <machine>: <text>`, the `keywork.creature.report` entry the thread reports use, so it reads on `GET /sessions/{id}` under `reports`), never a prompt: no turn starts, and it cannot approve, grant, change configuration or run anything. `node` names the receiving machine by StableID; omit it (or name this machine) for a creature here, which needs no pairing. Across machines it rides the tailnet listener of the node with the pair-key proof every paired request carries, so a machine this one has not paired is refused in words before anything is sent. The `inbound` policy of the receiving creature decides (`nobody`, `paired`, the default, or `{ named }`); a message may cross one machine (`hop`), a creature may send 12 an hour, a conversation takes 50 an hour, and the same words from the same sender within the hour are dropped. Every message is an audit row on both nodes (`message.send` here, `message.receive` where it lands; the text is only digested). The `origin` of the delivered line is `{ kind: "creature", creature: <sender>, thread: <message id>, node, machine }`.

from.description: The sending creature, on this machine.

node.description: The receiving machine's StableID; omitted, or this machine's own, for a creature here.

hop.description: How many machines the message that prompted this one had crossed; 0, the default, for a fresh message.

201.description: `{ delivered: { id, from, to, node, machine, hop } }`: `node` is the sender's machine, `machine` the name of the one it landed on.

400.description: The body is not a message, or it has crossed more machines than the hop limit allows; `error` says which.

403.description: The receiving creature's inbound policy refused the sender, or the machines are not paired; `error` says why in words.

404.description: No creature has that slug, here or on the receiving machine.

409.description: The same words from the same sender reached that creature within the hour; the repeat is dropped.

429.description: The sender or the receiving conversation reached its hourly limit.

502.description: The receiving machine did not answer, or does not take creature messages yet.

503.description: The mesh or creature messages are not served.

post.summary: The node hands this workspace a creature message that reached it over the tailnet after the pair proof held: `{ message: { id, from, to, text, hop }, caller: { stableId, name, userId, tags } }`, the caller as WhoIs named it, never as the sender claimed. The workspace runs it as a message that lands here through `POST /mesh/messages`: the inbound policy of the receiving creature, the hop, repeat and hourly limits, one line in its conversation and one `message.receive` audit row. A node that keeps its tailnet listener in another process than its workspaces posts each arrival here, trying the next workspace on 404.

400.description: The body is not an arrival, or the message has crossed more machines than the hop limit allows.

403.description: The inbound policy of the receiving creature refused the sender.

404.description: No creature here has that slug.

409.description: The message was already delivered, or the same words arrived within the hour.

429.description: The sender or the receiving conversation reached its hourly limit.

503.description: The mesh or creature messages are not served.

get.summary: The tailnet as this console sees it: `{ self, peers }`, each a machine `{ stableId, machine, dnsName, os, addresses, tags, user, online, active, candidate, path, node, manifest, endpoint? }`. Identity comes from `tailscale status` (`user` is null for a tagged machine); `path` is the lane (`direct`, `peer-relay`, `derp`, `offline`, `unknown`); `node` is the machine's unauthenticated `GET /mesh/hello` (`{ product, version, pairing }`), null when no keywork node answers or the peer is offline, shared in or expired; `endpoint` is the node's mesh base URL, the pair's when paired, else the address that answered. `manifest` is `{ roles }` from the node's manifest, which a node serves only to the consoles it is paired with, so it is null for every unpaired peer. `self` is this machine, with the manifest this node publishes.

502.description: Tailscale did not answer; `error` says why.

503.description: This node takes no tailnet census.

get.summary: The pairing attempts this console began with `POST /mesh/pairs` and has not finished: `{ pairings }`, each `{ attemptId, peerStableId, peerUserId, endpoint, role, caps, sas, confirmation, phase, startedAt, expiresAt }`. `sas` is the six-digit code to compare with the one the node shows; `confirmation` is what the node needs (`on-device`, `claim-code` or `endorsement`); `phase` is `comparing` until `POST /mesh/pairs/{id}/complete` is called, then `confirming` while the node's keeper confirms. An attempt leaves the list when it completes, is cancelled or expires; attempts live in this console's memory and end with it.

Every setting still out for the keeper, oldest first: `{ settings }`, each `{ id, creature, sessionId, what: { kind, ref, title }, rung, why, at, until, state, from, origin, replaces }`. A setting is one thing set out for the keeper to see: by the model working a session, with the `show` tool every served session carries (a plain conversation, a creature's conversation, a child, a chore run), or by the keeper's own hand, opening something from inside a setting or a thread (`POST /show`). It is IDE control: it arranges the console's own space, never the computer, so it asks no permission. `creature` is the creature's slug, or null for a session with no creature. `what.kind` is `file`, `diff`, `report`, `thread`, `chore`, `url` or `note`, and `what.ref` the workspace path, change-set id, report id, session id, chore id, url or the note's own words; `title` is absent when none was given. `rung` is what was proposed (`lantern`, `card`, `unfold` or `stage`); the console decides the rung it uses, through its yard. `why` is the one sentence for the card (empty for the keeper's own openings), `at` when it was set out, `until` when it goes (`seen`, `rests` or an ISO time) and `state` `live` or `pinned`. `from` is the id of the setting or the session it grew from, or null for one that starts a trail of its own; withdrawing or answering a setting never touches the settings that grew from it, so a console that folds them does so itself. `origin` is `creature` for what the model working a session set out, with or without a creature, and `keeper` for the keeper's own openings. `replaces` is the id of the setting this one replaced and withdrew (the same owner and the same thing, whoever set either out), or null, so a console moves what grew from the old id onto the new one. A console seats these on a cold start, as `GET /sessions` seats threads, then follows `show.proposed` and `show.settled` on the event stream. The server holds them in memory, so they outlive a console reconnecting but not the server. Since contract 1.27; `from`, `origin` and `replaces` since 1.28, and a console reading an older server takes their absence as `from: null`, `origin: "creature"` and `replaces: null`.

post.summary: Set out what the keeper opened from inside a setting or a thread (a file from a diff, a test from a file, a link), so every surface agrees on the trail. `what` is the thing, in the shape the `show` tool takes; `from` is the id of the setting still out, or of the session, it was opened from; `rung` is `unfold`, and may be left out. The keeper's own hand passes no gate and spends no budget: it never counts toward a creature's or a thread's hourly limit. The setting takes the thread and the creature of what it grew from (a setting's `sessionId` and `creature`, or the session itself and the creature it belongs to), with `why` empty, `until` `seen`, `from` as given and `origin` `keeper`, and `show.proposed` fires on that thread as for any setting. Opening the same thing again for the same owner replaces the earlier setting, which settles `withdrawn` by `keeper` first, and the new setting names it in `replaces`. Since contract 1.28.

kind.description: file, diff, report, thread, chore, url or note: what you set out.

ref.description: Which one: a workspace path for a file, a change-set id for a diff, a report id, a session id for a thread, a chore id, a url, or the note's own words (at most 2000 characters).

title.description: A short title for the card; the yard names it from ref when left out.

from.description: What the keeper opened it from: the id of a setting still out, or a session id.

201.description: `{ setting }` as it was set out.

400.description: The body is not `{ what: { kind, ref, title? }, from, rung? }` with `rung` `unfold`.

404.description: No setting still out and no session has the id in `from`.

post.summary: Record the keeper's answer to a setting and fire `show.settled` with `by: "keeper"` on the thread that set it out. `outcome` is `seen` (the keeper looked; it leaves the yard), `pinned` (it stays out, and the engine no longer withdraws it), `unpinned` (a pinned setting leaves, settled as seen) or `dismissed` (it leaves unread). Every keeper action on a setting posts here; a console settles nothing locally. Since contract 1.27.

200.description: `{ setting }` as it stands after the answer.

400.description: The body is not `{ outcome }` with `seen`, `pinned`, `unpinned` or `dismissed`.

404.description: No setting still out has that id.

409.description: The answer moves nothing: `unpinned` on a setting that is not pinned, or `seen` or `pinned` on one that is.
